rv.q: It is funny, witty and painfully aware — easily one of Rebeck's best works.
Rickman gives the comic performance of the season.
But Seminar is tight, witty and consistently entertaining, acquiring more muscle as the layers are peeled back to reveal both the scarred humanity and the numbness beneath Leonard's soured exterior.
Alan Rickman is heaven-sent as the sexy, sneering, snarling literary legend who condescends to tutor four aspiring novelists who have paid through the nose for the privilege of being abused.
The play's strength lies in its sharp dialogue and Alan Rickman's commanding performance as Leonard.
The play's saving grace is that it knows how to make us laugh.

But it can't sustain more than one thought or emotion or effect at the same time.
The play is funny in spots, but it's also deeply unpleasant, and not in a good way.
There are consolations, chief among them Rickman, who wisely understates Leonard's prickly intelligence, colossal ego, and enormous self-loathing.
But Higgins also offers some keen observations, highlighted in Trip Cullman’s fine production.
Yet Seminar, which opened Sunday at Broadway's Golden Theatre, is consistently clever and entertaining — and, under Sam Gold's briskly intelligent direction, a fine showcase for extraordinary actors.
The play's four aspiring writers are so uniformly awful—as people and as artists—that you can't help but wonder why Leonard bothers with them at all.
Leonard would have something barbed to say about him — and then approve.
